newsitem.title: UK: British forces foil N.Irish guerrilla attack.
newsitem.headline: British forces foil N.Irish guerrilla attack.

text.p: British forces foiled a planned Irish republican guerrilla landmine attack on a security patrol near the city of Londonderry, Northern Irish police said on Monday.
"It looks as if they were planning to blow up a patrol," an official said after police found preparations for what they believe was to be an ambush close to the border with the Irish Republic.
Security sources said it looked like the work of the Irish Republican Army (IRA), which resumed a war against British rule in Northern Ireland in February after a 17-month truce.
There was no comment from the outlawed group or from a dissident republican guerrilla organisation, the so-called Continuity IRA, which has been responsible for several abortive incidents since July.
The incident happened on Saturday but details were only released on Monday after two men were arrested and held for questioning about it.
Police sources said the culprits appeared to have escaped with their explosives but left behind a command wire, painted camouflage green, insulating tape and pliers.
The find was made after what was described as "suspicious activity" was detected in a rural area on the outskirts of Londonderry, a mainly nationalist city.
Security officials discovered a hole dug at the side of a road. "There was evidence that people had been lying concealed in shrubbery nearby," a police official told Reuters.
"They had been lying out for some time. It appears terrorists were planning a landmine attack."

The IRA struck at the heart of Britain's military presence in the province on October 7, exploding two car bombs that killed a soldier and wounded 30 other people at army headquarters in Lisburn, south of Belfast.
That attack marked the extension of a bombing campaign that began on mainland Britain in February, with bombs in London and Manchester. A British army base in Germany was also attacked.
Londonderry, Northern Ireland's second city, has been one of the main theatres of operation for the IRA during their 25-year campaign to oust Britain from the province.
Landmines dug into country road culverts and set off by command wires by hidden guerrillas have killed many British soldiers and police.

The latest aborted plan threw fresh doubts on a weekend report that the IRA has been operating an unofficial ceasefire since their October attack in Lisburn in an effort to win a seat at current multi-party peace talks for its political arm, Sinn Fein.
Last week British Defence Secretary Michael Portillo, on a visit to Lisburn garrison, said he saw no prospect of an early IRA truce.
